Brookfield Walks Away From Luxury L.A. Tower Rather Than Refinance
 
And, U.S. tax law classifies this upscale Miami neighborhood as “economically distressed”
 
By Craig Karmin
 

This is an edition of the Real Estate newsletter, a weekly briefing of the biggest commercial deals, news, analysis and trends in office, multifamily, retail and other commercial sectors. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 

Brookfield’s Beaudry apartment tower is a showpiece for downtown L.A. At 695 feet, it is among the tallest residential buildings in California and offers sweeping views of the city. Yet developer Brookfield this summer said it is walking away from the $600 million project, citing downtown L.A.’s “entrenched market challenges.” Brookfield is also exiting the property rather than refinancing the building’s roughly $360 million loan, which would have required tens of millions in additional costs because of today’s higher rates. Rebecca Picciotto reports on how rising interest rates are sending commercial real estate developers into retreat.

 

In Miami’s upscale Design District, shoppers carrying Dior and Chanel shopping bags stroll past valet lines packed with Bentleys and Ferraris. But under U.S. tax law, most of this 30-acre neighborhood is classified as an “economically distressed” community. Deborah Acosta explains why the way lawmakers drew up Opportunity Zones rules is sparking controversy.

 
 
 

They Built a $600 Million Luxury Tower in Downtown L.A. Now They’re Walking Away.

 
 
PAUL KIERNAN/WSJ
 

The Beaudry apartment tower is a visible showpiece for downtown L.A. 

 

Yet the developer, real-estate giant Brookfield, this summer said it is walking away from the $600 million project less than four years after it opened.

 
 
 
7.1%
 

The delinquency rate for multifamily loans in commercial mortgage-backed securities, up from 1% in October 2023, according to Morgan Stanley, as many owners struggle to afford refinancing costs.

 
 
 

Why This Upscale Miami District Is Designated a Distressed Opportunity Zone

 
 
SCOTT MCINTYRE FOR THE WALL STREET JOURNAL
 

In Miami’s upscale Design District, shoppers carrying Dior and Chanel shopping bags stroll past valet lines packed with Bentleys and Ferraris. Diners lounge at outdoor cafes, sipping $42 cocktails and nibbling on $82 branzino.

 

But under U.S. tax law, most of this 30-acre neighborhood is classified as an “economically distressed” community.

 
 
 

Data Points

 

• 196.5 million: The amount, in square feet, of industrial space available for sublease in the third quarter, according to Savills, a 13.6% year-over-year decline and positive sign for the sector as leasing rebounds despite rising interest rates.

 

• 23%: The year-over-year decline in restaurant acquisitions in the third quarter, the lowest level since the pandemic, according to CoStar’s BizBuySell. The slowdown reflects investor concern over the pressures facing restaurants and other small retail operators, including increased costs and a spending pullback by consumers.

 

• 2.7 million: The amount, in square feet, of life-sciences real estate leased in the third quarter, up 12.7% year-over-year, according to CBRE. The pickup in leasing hasn’t yet been enough to significantly lower the vacancy rate for the sector, which was overbuilt in the wake of the pandemic.
